segments.text: We turn today to Colossians chapter 3 and verse 14.
And beyond all these things put on love, which is the perfect bond of unity.
We were considering last week about the necessity for those who are chosen of God, verse 12,
to put on a heart of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience towards
one another.
The reason being that among those whom God has chosen to be in the body of Christ are people
of such different cultures, intellectual and social levels, and of different backgrounds.
As mentioned in verse 11, there are Greeks and Jews, barbarians and Scythians, slaves
and freemen, people of different communities, of different temperaments, different backgrounds,
different cultures.
And since none of these people whom God has chosen are perfect, none of us are perfect,
therefore there is a great need for us to put on towards each other a heart of compassion
and kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience.
Verse 13, bearing with one another, forgiving each other, whoever has a complaint against
anyone, forgive, just as the Lord's forgiven you.
It's very easy for us to have complaints against each other because of the flesh that each
of us have, in which, as Paul says, nothing good dwells.
And because of that, it is possible for us to hurt one another, consciously or unconsciously.
Very often, unconsciously.
And we must allow for that possibility that that person has hurt me in all likelihood
without knowing it.
And therefore, I need to forgive.
And then he comes on to this exhortation in verse 14.
Above all these things are, over all the rest, put on the robe of love, which he
says is the perfect bond of unity, or in other words, the link of the perfect life,
that which binds everything together in perfect harmony.
In other words, Paul is saying that if there is some other virtue that I have forgotten
to mention, well, it's all included in this one word, love.
And it also teaches us that the motive with which we are to be kind, gentle, patient,
and to bear with one another must be the motive of the divine love.
But it is possible for us to be kind and good towards one another, merely because civilization
and our culture has taught us to be like that.
And that's why he concludes with this exhortation in verse 14.
In other words, if we were to paraphrase verses 12 to 14 together, what Paul is really
saying is that your kindness towards one another must not be because your culture,
but because you have partaken of God's love.
In other words, from love must bring this kindness and this gentleness and this patience,
which teaches us that it is possible for us to have these virtues in our external behavior
without their springing from the divine nature within our hearts.
One of the characteristics of New Covenant living is what Jesus mentioned in John 738
as rivers of living water flowing from the innermost being.
The difference between the Old Covenant and the New Covenant, one difference anyway, is
that in the Old Covenant everything was in the external, but in the New Covenant it
has to flow from the innermost being.
In other words, it's not enough that I'm kind towards my brother.
That kindness must come out of love.
Otherwise, I have not entered into New Covenant life.
It's not enough that I am patient with my brother or that I hold my tongue and I do
not speak, retort in the same tone as he spoke to me.
That's not enough.
That patience and the control of my tongue must come from my innermost being.
It must come from love.
In other words, everything that's mentioned in verse 12 and 13 must spring out of a partaking
of God's nature in our hearts of the love of God.
For example, let's consider the matter of forgiveness mentioned in verse 13.
It's easy for us to externally go through the motions of forgiving someone who has
hurt us.
But if it has not sprung out from a heart of love towards that person who has hurt us,
you'll find that some weeks later or some months later that bitterness creeps up again
and you again have a problem with forgiving that person.
Again you find a complaint in your heart towards that person, even though some months
ago you went through the motion of forgiving.
And this is why the Word of God says, keep your heart with all diligence.
Verse 4, for out of the heart are the issues of life.
And so here in verse 14 he's speaking about the heart, about the motivation.
If our forgiveness and our kindness and our humility and our gentleness do not spring from
love, it's not perfect.
That's the meaning of verse 14.
Love is that perfect bond which binds all these things together in unity.
That is, there is something imperfect even in our compassion, our kindness, and our forgiving
one another.
And then he goes on to verse 15 where he says, let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts
to which indeed you were called in one body.
We must bear in mind that in this passage he's speaking about this calling that we have
in one body which he mentions in this verse.
You have been called in one body.
And that's what we considered in verse 11 that in this one body there are Greeks and
Jews, people of different backgrounds and temperaments and cultures and various different
levels of intellect, various social levels, etc.
But yet they've all been called in one body as chosen of God.
And in our relationships with one another, one test by which we can find out whether our
attitude towards our brothers and sisters is right and spiritual and divine is by checking
whether the peace of Christ is ruling in our hearts.
God has given us a conscience.
All men have a conscience.
But when we are born again and the Holy Spirit comes within, that conscience becomes sensitive
and the more we open up our mind and our heart to the teaching of God's word, our conscience
becomes more and more sensitive to the things that are divine, to God's standards.
And then we find that when we do something which violates God's laws, even though externally
there is no evidence of it, it may be a violation of God's law in our attitude inwardly towards
a brother.
God's law is a law of love.
We are to love our neighbor as ourselves.
And that is written in our hearts by the Holy Spirit.
That's the promise in the new covenant.
I will write my law in your heart and mind, says the Lord.
And when that law is written in our conscience, we find that our conscience becomes very sensitive
to the slightest violation of that law of love in our attitude.
And then what happens is we lose our peace.
And here Paul says the peace of Christ is like a referee.
That's another translation of this verse.
Let the peace of Christ be like a referee in your heart.
In a football game, a referee has a whistle.
And when he blows the whistle, that indicates that a foul has been committed.
And once a foul has been committed, it's no use running around with the football after
that because nothing counts after that point.
You've got to come back to the place where the foul has been committed and set the matter
right and then only proceed with the game.
Now it's exactly like that.
When it says here in verse 15, let the peace of Christ be like a referee in your heart.
That means when I lose my peace, that indicates something is wrong somewhere.
When there's unrest in my heart, something is wrong somewhere.
And it's no use continuing on.
I need to stop.
I need to stop whatever I'm doing.
And I ask the Lord and say, Lord, what's wrong?
I seem to have lost my peace.
And invariably, the Spirit of God will show us at that point where the foul has been
committed.
Some matter that was wrong, some attitude that was wrong, some word that was spoken
wrongly, something that needs to be set right, perhaps an apology to be made.
And then only will the peace of Christ return to our hearts.
So we need to be thankful that God has given us such a referee who blows a whistle, because
by this we are saved from wasting our life.
It's like pain.
Pain in the body indicates that something is wrong.
In fact, pain is one of the greatest blessings that our body has, because otherwise we'd never
know if something went wrong in our body.
But because pain indicates there's something wrong, we can check up and find out what
the cause of it is.
And usually it may be a disease or a sickness in exactly the same way.
Our conscience gives us pain and there is a lack of peace and unrest.
And that indicates that something is wrong.
And so we need to take this very seriously.
Let's take this matter of listening to that voice of conscience very seriously so that
whenever in future we come into unrest or lose that peace, we stop at what we're doing,
look up to God and ask Him to show us where we are wrong, set the foul right and proceed
on with our life.
We turn now to Colossians chapter 3 and verse 15.
We were considering in our last study about the peace of Christ acting as a referee in
our hearts, to which we have been called in one body.
Now this teaches us that if we allow the peace of Christ to be a faithful referee in each
of our hearts, it's really going to enable us to live together as one body.
We were considering in our last study that the peace of Christ is like a football referee
who blows the whistle when we have a wrong attitude towards another brother or someone
else in the body of Christ.
And so we find that if we listen to that voice, listen to the referee blowing the
whistle and seek to set the foul right immediately, the result will be that we always live in
a good relationship with one another.
We put on love in our attitudes towards one another, forgiving each other, bearing with
one another, forgiving all complaints, having a heart of compassion, kindness, humility
and all the other things mentioned in verses 12 to 14.
For the peace of Christ, this unrest that comes in our heart, is the referee blowing
the whistle, the peace of Christ, the referee blowing the whistle, that something's wrong.
Now the reason why we find very often Christians are unable to get along with each other is
because each of them has not been faithful to listen to the voice of the referee blowing
the whistle in their hearts.
The secret of a good relationship, whether it is between a husband and wife, as he goes
on to speak of in verses 18 and 19, or in the body of Christ between brothers and brothers,
or between brothers and sisters, or sisters and sisters, the secret of it all is where
each person follows this exhortation to allow the peace of Christ to be the referee in
their hearts.
Thus we can be one body.
And another thing he goes on to say in our relationships with one another is this matter
of being thankful in the last part of verse 15.
Be thankful.
Of course, we need to be thankful to God for all His blessings, thankful to God that He
makes everything work together for our good according to Romans 8.28.
And all the other wonderful things that God blesses us with and does for us and speaks
to us from His word, we need to be thankful.
We need to be thankful for forgiveness of sins, for the gift of the Holy Spirit, for the hope
that we have laid up for us in the future and all that.
But in the context here, it is particularly referring to being thankful for one another
in the body of Christ.
For as we considered right on from verse 11, he is speaking about our calling in the
body of Christ, the different types of people that there are in the body listed in verse
And all these, verse 12, have been chosen of God, and their attitudes towards one another
is described in verses 12, 13, and 14.
And in order to maintain that attitude, verse 15, we need to listen to the peace of Christ,
which is the referee in our hearts.
And thus we become one body functionally.
And therefore, in that context, this exhortation, be thankful, refers to being thankful for one
another.
Now, it's easy for the Greek to be thankful for the fellow Greek and for the Jew to be
thankful for the fellow Jew.
It's easy for the cultured person to be thankful for another cultured person and for the
barbarian to be thankful for another barbarian.
It's a little more difficult when we seek to be thankful for others who are different
from us, a different community, different intellectual level, different temperament,
different caste, culture, race, different social level, because they have so many things so
completely different from us that we find as much that we have to bear with and forgive.
But it's not enough to bear with and forgive.
That's just the first step.
He has told us to bear with one another in verse 13 and to forgive each other, but he
goes on to a higher step, and this is the mark of real love, that we are thankful.
We can think of marital relationships, a husband and wife.
To love one another does not mean merely that the husband and wife put up with each
other and bear with each other.
Of course, that's necessary, but that's only the beginning.
To really love one another means that a husband and wife are thankful for one another, thankful
to God for giving them to each other.
In the same way, we need to be thankful to God for giving us these brothers and sisters
in the body of Christ.
Here is an area of great lack among many Christians.
It's quite likely there are many believers who have never once in their life thanked
God for their fellow believers in their church fellowship.
That's a sad lack.
And when we are not thankful, it's very easy for Satan to come and bring a misunderstanding,
a division, and some type of separation between those who are called to be one body in
Christ.
And so let's take this exotation seriously.
Be thankful.
And if you look at the other brothers and sisters whom God has put you together with in your
fellowship, I'm sure you'll be able to discover something in them that you can thank God
for.
We don't have to pretend that they are spiritual if they are not, but we can certainly thank
God for something that we can find in them, if not for anything else, at least for the
fact that their sins are forgiven, that they have turned and accepted Christ, and that
God has accepted them.
And if God has accepted them, there's no reason why we shouldn't, just as they are.
God doesn't wait till they become perfect before accepting them, neither should we wait
till they become perfect before we accept them.
God is thankful for them, and we need to be thankful for them too.
In the Old Testament, in the book of Zephaniah, there is a verse, not very well known, but
a very good verse, Zephaniah 3, verse 17, where it says that the Lord rejoices
over His people with shouts of joy.
It's a tremendous verse when we think that God rejoices over His children who are so imperfect
in so many ways with shouts of joy.
To think that God could rejoice over imperfect people is really a challenge to us.
We ourselves are imperfect, and God rejoices over us and accepts us.
We need to rejoice over our brothers and sisters and be thankful to God for them.
This is the secret of fellowship, to be thankful for one another.
And so when we read verse 15, we find new meaning in it now.
Let the peace of Christ act as a referee in your heart.
To this you have been called in one body, and be thankful for one another in the body
of Christ.
Whatever their limitations, whatever their faults.
Practice thanksgiving, or as another translation puts it, learn to be grateful and practice
being thankful and show yourselves thankful.
In other words, express your thanksgiving to one another.
And then in verse 16, he says, let the word of Christ dwell in you richly.
That is, the word particularly in the New Testament, the word of Christ refers particularly
to that which has come to us in the New Testament, Jesus Christ being the mediator of the New
Covenant.
Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you.
That cannot dwell within us unless we take time to read and meditate on it.
Thus it can dwell richly within us.
Thus it can be our strength in the moments of temptation, because the word of God richly
dwells in Jesus, He could use it when He was tempted by Satan.
With all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another, when God's word dwells in us richly,
then we can teach and admonish one another.
It is God's will that we learn to teach and admonish one another even if we are not called
to be teachers, not all are called to be teachers, but yet every one of us can have
a ministry of encouraging and challenging one another.
But that's only possible if the word of Christ is dwelling richly within us.
In all wisdom we are to teach and admonish one another.
There is a great need for wisdom in the way we seek to share God's word to help and encourage
others, not in a condemnatory type of way, but in an encouraging, challenging way.
And so wisdom is required, not just knowledge.
Let the word of Christ dwell richly within you, it says, and with all wisdom teaching
and admonishing one another, God's word is meant to make us wise, and with that wisdom
we can help others.
And he goes on to say that we are to do this with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs,
singing with thankfulness in your hearts to God.
We can admonish one another through the hymns that we sing.
There are two types of hymns that we can sing.
One, hymns of praise to God, as it says in the last part of verse 16, singing with
thankfulness in your hearts to God.
The other is hymns of exhorting one another or challenging one another to press on to follow
in the footsteps of Christ.
And we find that singing and praising have a very important place in the life of the
believer.
And those who have the word of Christ dwelling richly within them will find a song of praise
in their hearts.
David says in Psalm 14, Thou hast put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God.
And this is one of the marks of the word of God having produced its effect in our lives.
So let's take this exhortation seriously, that the word of Christ will dwell richly
within us, producing within us a song of praise to God and wisdom to exhort and challenge
others around us.
We turn today to Colossians chapter 3 and verse 16.
We were considering in our last few studies the relationships that should exist between
fellow believers in the body of Christ.
And this section begins in verse 11 about the various types of people that are in the
body, the attitude they should have towards one another, verse 12, 13 and 14, the peace
of Christ that acts as a referee in our hearts, verse 15, to protect us in our mutual
relationship, thankfulness for one another, and then the teaching, exhorting, admonishing
relationship that it should exist mutually within one another in the body of Christ in
verse 16.
Notice in verse 16 that it says we are to teach and admonish one another.
It's not just a question of one person getting up as the teacher and teaching everybody else
or exhorting everybody else.
The New Testament places great emphasis on a body ministry.
There is no one-man ministry taught in the New Testament.
That is a tradition of men that has hindered the building up of the body in many places.
In Hebrews 3 verse 13 we are told to encourage or exhort one another daily.
Again, the emphasis is on one another, just like love one another or forgive one another.
Is there any one person who is supposed to do all the loving?
Is there any one person who is supposed to do all the forgiving?
No.
In exactly the same way when it says, teach and admonish one another, Colossians 3.16,
or exhort and encourage one another, Hebrews 3.13, or Hebrews 10.25, exhort and encourage
one another again, it must mean that God's will is not, that one person should do
all the exhorting and all the admonishing and all the teaching.
God's will is that we learn to exhort and encourage one another.
When you turn to 1 Corinthians 14 and verse 26, Paul envisages the whole church coming
together and each one having a psalm, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, and an interpretation
in 1 Corinthians 14 verse 26.
Thus each person has something to contribute to the building up of the other.
And there is a great need for this type of body ministry if we are to see the body of
Christ being expressed and manifested in local situations.
And so that phrase in Colossians 3.16, one another, is a very important phrase.
Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you with all wisdom, teaching and admonishing
one another.
And this admonition may not be with some profound teaching from God's word, it can
be with a psalm, it can be with a song, or as it says in 1 Corinthians 14.26, with

There are many ways by which we can exhort one another, but with thankfulness in our

And in verse 17 we are told a fundamental law for everything that we do in our
Christian life.
Whatever you do, he says in verse 17, in word or in deed, do all in the name of
the Lord Jesus, giving thanks through Him to God the Father.
So here is a law for every single thing that we do.
The verse in 1 Corinthians chapter 10 has some relation to this.
1 Corinthians chapter 10 verse 31 we are told, whether then you eat or drink, or
whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
Everything that we do must be done for the glory of God.
That's one law.
That is not done for the glory of God, is not done in a Christian way.
The same thing we see in 1 Peter 4.11, in everything let God be glorified through
Jesus Christ.
Here in Colossians 3.17 we are told that everything must be done in the name of
the Lord Jesus, and everything must be done giving thanks to God the Father.
Now if we were to follow this principle and check all our actions and words, for
that's what it says in Colossians 3.17, we would find that there are many things
that we need to get rid of.
Much cleansing needs to take place in our conversational habits, for all our words
must be spoken in the name of the Lord Jesus.
In other words, in our conversation there must be nothing that we are ashamed of,
nothing that we would have to hold back if Jesus himself were sitting, listening
to what we were saying.
That's part of the meaning of doing it all in the name of the Lord Jesus.
For the glory of God means that we do not seek our own honor or glory in anything
that we speak or in anything that we do.
And giving thanks through Jesus Christ to God the Father indicates that there must
be nothing which we do with a grumbling, grudging spirit.
For example, it says in 1 Peter 4 that we are to show hospitality towards one another
without grudging.
Whatever we do, we have to do it with thankfulness.
If we give to God, we must give with thankfulness without grudging.
And so this is a very good law, a very good verse by which we could check whether what
we are doing measures up to God's standard or not.
We shall discover in the final day of judgment that the motive and the attitude with which
we did our actions were a million times more important than the actions themselves.
And so if we make it a habit and a practice to check in our lives day by day whether our
words and deeds measure up to the standard given here in Colossians 3.17 and 1 Corinthians
10.31, can I do this in the name of the Lord Jesus?
Can I do this for the glory of God, giving thanks to the Father?
If so, let me go ahead and do it.
Otherwise, let me avoid it.
So many questions that young people have concerning whether they can do this and whether they
can do that are all resolved when we ask ourselves these questions mentioned in 1 Corinthians
10.31 and Colossians 3.17, basically three questions.
Is this for the glory of God?
Second, can I do this in the name of the Lord Jesus?

If what I'm planning to do or what I'm planning to say or what I'm planning to write fails
in one of these three tests, it's best avoided.
It's a doubtful thing and it's best avoided.
And if we make it a habit in our life to check what we do by this three-fold test, we'll
find that a real cleansing takes place in our life and spiritual growth as a result.
Again, we were considering that all this was in the context of one body.
In other words, in our relationships with one another, if we do everything we do to

Having spoken of that, Paul goes on to another aspect of the building of the body of Christ,

He speaks about wives and husbands in verses 18 and 19, children and parents in verses 20

to see that here is where the attack is and here is where God seeks to lead us

We turn to Colossians chapter 3 and verse 18 today.
